changes.before: Configure the search form to GET /search, send the topic under q, and send includeNotes=yes only while its checkbox is checked.
changes.after: Choose where form values go and which names they use.

before: A form’s action names the destination. Its method chooses how to send the data.
GET places form data in the URL query and suits a search that retrieves information. POST usually sends data in the request body and is used for actions that change state.
POST is not encryption. Use HTTPS and appropriate server protections for private information; do not put secrets in a search URL.
The name attribute supplies a submitted key. The id connects labels and identifies an element, but it does not replace name.

An unchecked checkbox contributes no name-value pair. A checked checkbox uses its name and value.
```html
<input type="checkbox" name="images" value="yes">
```
Disabled controls and controls without a name are normally omitted from submitted form data. A visible label alone does not submit its text.
The practice checks FormData locally without sending a network request. A working /search route would still be needed to return results.
after: A form’s `action` is the address that receives its data. Its `method` says how to send that data.

`GET` puts the form values in the page address, after a `?`. It suits a search. `POST` usually puts the values in the request’s body instead of the address. It is often used when an action saves or changes something.
`POST` does not hide data by itself. HTTPS protects data while it travels. Keep private information out of search addresses, which can be saved in browser history.
A field’s `name` is the key sent with its value. Its `id` connects the field to a label. Changing one does not automatically change the other.

A checkbox sends its value only when it is checked.

```html
<input type="checkbox" name="images" value="yes">
```

`type` makes a checkbox. `name="images"` gives its data key. When checked, it sends `images=yes`. When unchecked, it sends no pair for that key.
A disabled field is normally left out of the sent data. So is a field with no `name`. A label helps people understand the field, but its words are not the field’s data key.

Change the form to `method="get"` and keep `action="/search"`. Give the topic field `name="q"`. Give the checkbox `name="includeNotes"` and `value="yes"`. The checks inspect the data locally. They do not send it, and this practice has no search service to return results.

before.question: An input has id="email", a matching label and the value learner@example.org, but no name. What happens in ordinary form submission?
choices: It sends email=learner@example.org because id is the key
It sends the label text as the key
Its value is omitted because it has no submitted name
before.explanation: id connects the label and element. Form submission uses name for the key; without one this input contributes no pair.

after.question: An input has an id, a label and a typed value, but no name. What does it send?
choices: Nothing. It needs a name to send that value.
after.explanation: The id connects the label. The name supplies the data key. A field without a name is left out.

before: Choose the method appropriate for retrieving search results.
The topic id can stay topic while its submitted name is q.
Set the checkbox’s name and value; do not force it to stay checked.
after: Keep the topic field’s id as topic so its label still works.
You do not need to submit the form to pass the checks.
